content: The 2020 WHO consolidated guidelines on tuberculosis preventive treatment were developed to provide updated recommendations for healthcare professionals and policymakers working on tuberculosis (TB), HIV, infectious diseases, and maternal and child health. These guidelines build upon the 2018 edition, incorporating new evidence from clinical trials on shorter rifamycin-containing preventive regimens. The primary objectives were to enhance the clarity and global applicability of the recommendations and to reflect the latest evidence. The guidelines replace previous WHO policy documents on managing latent TB infection (LTBI) in people living with HIV (PLHIV), household contacts of TB patients, and other high-risk groups. They were prepared following the requirements of the Guideline Review Committee, with the Guideline Development Group (GDG) evaluating the quality of evidence on effectiveness, harms, certainty, values, preferences, equity, resource use, acceptability, and feasibility. The GDG also considered the implications of evidence for specific at-risk population subgroups, their likelihood of progressing from infection to active TB, and the incidence of active TB compared to the general population. The GDG emphasized that the individual benefit of preventive treatment outweighs the risks, particularly for LTBI testing and TB preventive treatment (TPT). LTBI testing is recommended whenever feasible to identify individuals at the highest risk of developing active TB. Additional resources required for implementing the guidance should not be seen as barriers but as opportunities to mobilize appropriate funding levels. The guidelines include 18 recommendations covering critical steps in the programmatic management of TB preventive treatment (PMTPT). These steps follow the cascade of preventive care: identifying at-risk populations (e.g., PLHIV, household contacts), ruling out active TB disease, testing for LTBI, providing treatment, and monitoring adverse events, adherence, and treatment completion. Most recommendations from the 2018 update remain unchanged, but the 2020 guidelines introduce new options, such as a 1-month daily rifapentine and isoniazid regimen and a 4-month daily rifampicin regimen, as alternative TPT options in all settings under specific conditions. The updated guidelines also include advice on isoniazid preventive treatment during pregnancy and the concurrent use of rifapentine and dolutegravir, reflecting findings from recent studies. Recommendations previously restricted by national TB incidence thresholds are now applicable to any country, subject to setting-specific conditions. Operational limitations that countries must urgently address to achieve global targets are highlighted. The publication of the new guidelines will be followed by an operational guide providing practical details for programmatic implementation. These documents are part of a modular set of consolidated guidelines and operational guides that integrate other WHO normative documents on TB. Key recommendations include: 1. Adults and adolescents living with HIV who are unlikely to have active TB should receive TPT as part of comprehensive HIV care, regardless of antiretroviral therapy (ART) status, pregnancy, or previous TB treatment history, even if LTBI testing is unavailable. 2. Infants under 12 months living with HIV and in contact with a TB patient should receive TPT if active TB is ruled out. 3. Children aged 12 months or older living with HIV in high TB transmission settings should be offered TPT as part of comprehensive HIV care, regardless of TB contact history. 4. All children living with HIV who have completed TB treatment may receive TPT. 5. Children under 5 years who are household contacts of bacteriologically confirmed pulmonary TB patients should receive TPT, even if LTBI testing is unavailable. 6. Older children, adolescents, and adults who are household contacts of confirmed TB patients may also be given TPT if active TB is excluded. 7. Preventive treatment may be considered for high-risk household contacts of multidrug-resistant TB patients based on individualized risk assessment and clinical justification. 8. Systematic LTBI testing and treatment are recommended for individuals initiating anti-TNF treatment, receiving dialysis, preparing for organ or hematological transplants, or with silicosis. 9. Systematic LTBI testing and treatment may be considered for prisoners, healthcare workers, immigrants from high TB burden countries, homeless individuals, and people who use drugs. 10. Systematic LTBI testing and treatment are not recommended for people with diabetes, harmful alcohol use, tobacco smokers, or underweight individuals unless they belong to other high-risk groups. For LTBI testing, either a tuberculin skin test (TST) or interferon-gamma release assay (IGRA) can be used. Recommended TPT options include 6 or 9 months of daily isoniazid, a 3-month weekly rifapentine plus isoniazid regimen, a 3-month daily isoniazid plus rifampicin regimen, a 1-month daily rifapentine plus isoniazid regimen, or 4 months of daily rifampicin alone. In high TB transmission settings, PLHIV with unknown or positive LTBI test results and no active TB should receive at least 36 months of daily isoniazid preventive therapy (IPT), regardless of ART status, immunosuppression, previous TB treatment, or pregnancy. The guidelines also harmonize decision points for LTBI testing and TPT, simplify treatment durations, and update content with recent evidence, such as the use of rifapentine with dolutegravir and isoniazid preventive treatment in pregnant women with HIV. Research gaps have been updated to reflect the latest evidence reviewed. These guidelines aim to support the development of national LTBI management guidelines tailored to local circumstances and to expand population-level LTBI treatment coverage, which remains low even in priority target groups.
